newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Merrill exec says mergers to continue.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Merrill exec says mergers to continue.

text.p: Mergers between financial services firms such as the deal just struck between Morgan Stanley and Dean Witter would continue as the industry rationalised into global giants, senior Merrill Lynch and Co Inc executive Win Smith said on Thursday.
"We think there is an endgame going on in financial services, not only in the United States but around the world," said Smith at a press briefing here.
"Consolidation is, if anything, accelerating," said Smith, who is chairman of Merrill Lynch International and a member of the executive committee of Merrill Lynch and Co.
The surprise US$10.2 billion merger of the Morgan Stanley Group Inc. and Dean Witter Discover and Co was announced during Wednesday afternoon trade on Wall Street.

Analysts said the merger would form a Wall Street brokerage firm that rivalled Merrill Lynch in size and spread, with the deal neatly joining Morgan Stanley's strength in investment banking and Dean Witter's strong retail presence.
The analysts said the merger could spark another round of industry takeovers, citing Lehman Bros Holdings Inc and Painewebber Group Inc as potential targets.
While Merrill would continue to rank as the largest firm in terms of revenues, it would be eclipsed by the merger as the leader in asset management, they also said.

Smith, who is visiting Australia following Merrill's A$117 million purchase of local broker McIntosh Securities Ltd, said the Morgan Stanley/Dean Witter deal was a validation of the company's strategy.

"... having a global franchise and having a leading position in both the capital markets/investment banking sector as well as the private client sector is going to be the necessary model to compete on a global basis."
He said there was little room in the competitive marketplace these days for niche players, although some specialised firms had a role to play.

"But if you are going to compete worldwide now you have to have a number of key attributes. And we think that probably half a dozen to 10-12 firms are going to be able to pull that together by the end of the decade and we certainly intend to be one of those," Smith said.

Merrill Lynch, which had total net revenue of US$13.12 billion in 1996, had placed a lot of emphasis on expansion outside the United States in the last five years to meet the requirements of clients and to take advantage of the lowering of international regulatory barriers.
Smith said 7,500 of the company's 50,000 employees are based outside the U.S., with about 30 percent of net revenues from non-U.S. sources.
